provenance: PR #29 R21. Three times in this PR a published wall-clock band failed to match the `evals/report/history.jsonl` committed beside it: nine of fifteen runs published as 'every run the ledger records', four values that appear in no recorded run at that case count, the two slowest `invariant` runs dropped unlabelled, and a ceiling derived from a maximum (64.71s) that was never measured. Nothing graded any of it, which is why prose drifted that far — and the same selective-band presentation is what ADR-013 Decision 4 was withdrawn over. This grades the PROPERTY, not the snapshot: `history.jsonl` grows on every gate run, so a check that string-matched the published list would go red on the next run rather than on a regression. It asserts that the doc's case count is the current one, that the committed ceiling is at least ADR-013's rule applied to the ledger's slowest run at that count, and that the published number derives that same ceiling. The last one is deliberately `rule(published) == rule(ledger max)` rather than the stricter `published >= ledger max` the reviewer proposed: the harmful failure R21 found is a band that justifies a LOWER ceiling than the truth (12.96s published where 13.57s was recorded, giving 15 where the rule said 20), and the strict form reddens on ordinary variance instead — this tree moved 0.2-0.5s between consecutive runs while the check was being written, which would make the doc need re-editing after every slightly slow run. That is the same rot-by-construction trap in a different place, so the property graded is the one that matters. T-R34 added two halves to the same check, both from the drift that produced that task: README's band-table row must carry the SAME case count and maximum as ADR-019's sentence (the two documents drifted apart in PR #29 R24 and only the ADR was graded), and a suite may publish exactly one band line -- the parse is a dict comprehension over `finditer`, so a superseded line left in the file used to shadow the live one in silence. PR #35 R2 and R4 added the two halves the round-1 version still missed: README's row parse was the same last-wins dict comprehension the ADR side had just been guarded against (stale rows ABOVE live rows left it green with two contradictory bands per suite), and nothing read the ceiling the ADR DERIVES in prose -- so a band re-measured downwards after a case was added could argue `-> **15**` under a heading that says 20s. The derivation sentence must now multiply the published maximum, be arithmetically right, and land on `WALL_BUDGET_S[suite]`. PR #35 R5 added the third: the published number must BE a row in the ledger recorded with nothing uncommitted in the tree (`dirty: false`). Round 1 published both bands off runs that were red AND dirty -- a band justified by a tree that was never committed. Green is deliberately NOT required and cannot be: this check is in both suites, so at a new case count every run is red until the band is republished and no green row could ever exist to republish it from (T-R53 carries that half). `evals/run.py` had to be fixed in the same round for a clean row to be producible at all -- `dirty` was read AFTER the report file was written, so every `--report` run recorded itself as dirty on account of its own untracked artifact. PR #35 R11 then found the `dirty: false` requirement deadlocked the one operation CLAUDE.md rule 2 makes routine: a tree only reaches count N+1 while the new case is uncommitted, so every row at N+1 is dirty until the commit the check was blocking. The band sentence now cites its run by ledger timestamp and cleanliness is judged AS OF that run -- a dirty row is refused only when a clean one was already available when the band was published. That is stable in both directions: it cannot deadlock the bootstrap, and later clean rows cannot retroactively redden a published band. R13 added the derivation's precision and the requirement that the stated arrow is `_band_rule(x)`; the separate claim that the ADR's advertised ceiling is the committed one moved to the Ruling line, because the rule applied to a fresh short sample legitimately comes out below the committed ceiling (12.89s at 53 cases gives 15 against a committed 20) and tying them together would have re-created R11's deadlock by another route. T-R56 folded two more properties into the same check, both from the same class of defect — a document describing a rule the code does not implement. T-R55: the `fast` band cited a row the ledger records as 134/136 and said nothing about it, while `invariant`'s citation disclosed 53/53, so a reader comparing the two would read the silence as a pass. The band sentence now carries the cited row's own `passed/total` and item 2 grades it — green is still required nowhere, which is exactly why the result has to be stated. T-R46/T-R47: §6 claimed to be the one place the rules are stated while two of its own paragraphs restated item 2, README restated items 3 and 7, and two keys this check's sibling emits were still on the `property N` numbering PR #35 round 4 retired — an off-by-one against §6's list in a red report. The restatements now defer by number and item 8 grades that the deferrals resolve: the list is 1..N with no gaps, and every `item N` in ADR-019, README or the check's own source names one of them, under that name. That is the structural half — a blacklist of retired phrases cannot catch a restatement that is correct today and stale next round, but a reference that stops resolving is red. PR #36 R1 then falsified the claim this section had been making about itself: 'one list, in one place ... stated nowhere else' was asserted in ADR-019, INDEX.md and this check's docstring while the same commit added restatements to all three. The claims are narrowed to what item 8 (references) actually grades — every reference names an item that exists and spells its slug — and the residue (an unreferenced paraphrase) is stated as ungraded rather than denied. PR #36 R10/R11 then found the narrowed claim overstating in turn: the Graded half promised a reference 'names an item that exists AND spells its slug' while a bare name for a nonexistent item was green, and promised the list carried slugs while a slugless trailing item was invisible. Both are graded now, and §6's Graded paragraph is written clause by clause against the mutations that hold it up.

triage.note: tagged invariant. The cost is deliberate and is the same one `docs-numbers-are-derived` charges: a run slower than the published band reddens the next gate run until the band is re-measured, and adding a case to a suite reddens it until the band is re-measured at the new count. A band nobody re-measures is the thing that produced R21.
triage.watched_red: three ways, each against the defect it rules out. (1) Against the text as PR #29 R21 found it — ADR-019 publishing `invariant` 12.96s and `fast` 64.71s — the check reports {suite: invariant, published_slowest: 12.96, ledger_slowest: 13.57, ceiling: 15, required_by_adr013_rule: 20} and {suite: fast, published_slowest: 64.71, ledger_slowest: 65.14}: a maximum that was in no recorded run, and a ceiling the rule had never justified. (2) With the committed `invariant` ceiling put back to 15 against the current ledger: {suite: invariant, ceiling: 15, required_by_adr013_rule: 20, ledger_slowest: 14.12}. (3) Before ADR-019 carried any band line at all: {suite: fast, adr_publishes_no_band_line: true} and the same for invariant. It also went red for real, unplanned, during this commit's own preparation: a 66.50s `fast` run landed after the band was published at 65.53s, and the next gate run reported it — which is the behaviour, not a defect. T-R34's two additions were watched red the same way: editing README's `fast` row to 66.05s against an ADR that says 66.38s gives {suite: fast, adr_band: [133, 66.38], readme_band: [133, 66.05]}; deleting README's `invariant` row gives {suite: invariant, adr_band: [52, 13.22], readme_band: null}; and adding a second `Slowest recorded `invariant` run at 52 cases` line gives {suite: invariant, adr_publishes_two_band_lines: true} plus the README disagreement the shadowing line caused. PR #35 R2/R4, three more, each the reviewer's own reproduction. Stale 132/66.33 and 51/14.12 rows inserted ABOVE README's live rows: [{suite: fast, readme_publishes_two_bands: true}, {suite: invariant, readme_publishes_two_bands: true}]. The band re-measured down to 12.80s with §3 and README following it: [{suite: invariant, published_slowest: 12.8, derives_ceiling: 15, ledger_slowest: 13.22, ledger_derives: 20, runs: 13}, {suite: invariant, derivation: [12.8, 14.7, 15], arithmetic: 14.7, committed_ceiling: 20}] -- the second entry is the new one, and it is the state R4 showed was reachable with everything else green. Breaking the arithmetic alone (`66.38 x 1.15 = 66.3`): [{suite: fast, derivation: [66.38, 66.3, 80], arithmetic: 76.3, committed_ceiling: 80}]. R5 watched red against exactly what round 1 shipped: republishing `invariant`'s band from ts 20260823-023204 (13.22s, `passed: 50, total: 52, dirty: true`) gives {suite: invariant, published: 13.22, is_not_a_clean_recorded_run_at: 52}. PR #35 R11/R13, four more. Publishing one decimal, `13.08 × 1.15 = 15.0 → **20**`: [{suite: invariant, adr_row: [52, 13.08, 15.04, 20], readme_row: [52, 13.08, 15.0, 20]}, {suite: invariant, derivation: [13.08, 15.0, 20], arithmetic: 15.04, rule_gives: 20, committed_ceiling: 20}]. A band whose rule does NOT give the stated ceiling (`13.04 × 1.15 = 14.996 → **20**`): {suite: invariant, derivation: [13.04, 14.996, 20], arithmetic: 15.0, rule_gives: 15, ...} plus the citation and row mismatches it drags with it. Citing a ts that is not a row at this count, and citing a row whose wall clock is not the published number, each name themselves (cites_no_recorded_run / actually_measured). And the Ruling line edited to advertise a ceiling nothing commits: {suite: invariant, adr_ruling_ceiling: 15, committed_ceiling: 20}. T-R56, three more, each the mutation its acceptance names. (1) The `fast` band citation rewritten to claim 136/136 for the row the ledger records as 134/136: {suite: fast, cited_run: 20260823-161401, citation_claims: '136/136', row_records: '134/136'}. (2) Before the band sentences carried a result at all, the parse found no band line and the check reported {suite: fast, adr_publishes_no_band_line: true} + the same for invariant — the bootstrap red, watched first. (3) A README sentence deferring to a §6 item that does not exist — watched first as {readme: cites_no_such_six_item, items: [9], list_is_1_to: 7} under the number-only guard that round shipped; that key no longer exists, and the same mutation prints {readme: reference_does_not_name_its_item, wrote: 'item 9', item_9_is: null} now; and the two retired keys restored in `_check_published_band_slack`: {eval_adapter: uses_the_retired_property_numbering, found: ['2', '3']}. The list's own numbering was mutated too — item 7 renumbered to 9, leaving a gap: red then as {adr_six_list_is_not_1_to_n: ['1','2','3','4','5','6','9','8']}, and now under the key that replaced it, which carries each item's slug beside its number. And item 5 deleted from the middle of the list, references untouched: red on the list shape and on every reference below the hole. Inserting an item mid-list was NOT caught at that point; PR #36 R2 made it, and the whole class of mis-aimed references, red — see below. The cold review of this task (F1/F3) forced two more. The rule's rate re-typed as an amendment would make — `_BAND_RATE` 1.15 -> 1.20 with the documents untouched — is red on the stale documents rather than green on them: [{suite: fast, published_slowest: 62.44, derives_ceiling: 75, ledger_slowest: 63.15, ledger_derives: 80}, {suite: fast, adr_row: [136, 62.44, 74.93, 80], readme_row: [136, 62.44, 71.81, 80]}, {suite: invariant, adr_row: [...15.98...], readme_row: [...15.32...]}, {suite: fast, no_derivation_of: 62.44}, {suite: invariant, no_derivation_of: 13.32}] — before that repair the check re-typed 1.15 three times and stayed green on all of it. And the docstring's own count of the properties, which said seven while the list said eight: not a red, a finding, and the count is gone rather than corrected. PR #36 R1/R2 — the round that found this repair carrying its own defect class. The falsification first, watched green where it should have been red: re-pointing README's `§6 item 3` at item 6, an unrelated rule, left `_check_published_band()['passed'] == True` with `wrong == []`, because 6 is a number the list has and position was all that was graded. §6's items now carry a stable slug and every reference spells both, so the same mutation is {readme: reference_does_not_name_its_item, wrote: 'item 6 (same-ceiling)', item_6_is: 'ruling'}. Renumbering the list under its references — an item inserted at position 3, every reference left alone — is red on 20+ shapes at once, e.g. {adr: reference_does_not_name_its_item, wrote: 'item 3 (same-ceiling)', item_3_is: 'green'} and {wrote: 'item 4 (committed-ceiling)', item_4_is: 'same-ceiling'}: that is T-R59 closed in the same mechanism rather than carried. What is still NOT graded, and is now stated that way in ADR-019 §6, README and this check's docstring instead of being claimed away: a paragraph that paraphrases a rule and names no item at all (T-R62). Re-slugging the mutation honestly (`item 6 (ruling)`) is green — a correct reference in a wrong sentence is prose, and no mechanism here reads prose. R5's false-positive direction was watched too: `{"missing_item_9": x}`, `line_item_12` and `my_items_4` all matched the old `[ _]` separator and would have reddened the gate from anywhere in this 3,900-line adapter; the separator is a space and the scan is the marked band region, so all three now match nothing. One more, unplanned and self-inflicted, which is the finding worth keeping: the marked region this check reads its own file through was delimited by two constants holding the marker text verbatim, so `split` found the closing marker inside its own tuple and the region was the 68 lines between the opening marker and that definition — 456 lines of band code unscanned, check green. Building the markers instead of quoting them brought the region back and immediately reddened five references the rewrite had broken (`item 7 (readme-` wrapped mid-slug, `§6 item 3 (above, ...)`, two slugs continued behind a comment marker): {eval_adapter: reference_does_not_name_its_item, wrote: 'item 7', item_7_is: 'readme-row'} and four like it. A comment pointed at the wrong item is red the same way a document is: {eval_adapter: reference_does_not_name_its_item, wrote: 'Item 4 (derivation)', item_4_is: 'committed-ceiling'}. PR #36 R10/R11/R12 — the round that found the round-1 repair had deleted a guard it still advertised. Each is watched from its own falsification. R10: `slugs.get(n) != slug` is `None != None` for a BARE reference to an item that does not exist, so README's `§6 item 9 is why …` returned {passed: True, wrong: []} — the exact input the previous round's code had reported. Now: {readme: reference_does_not_name_its_item, wrote: 'item 9', item_9_is: null}. R11: the list was read through a slug-bearing pattern, so a slugless item was absent from it, and an absent LAST item left 1..N intact — appending `9. a brand new rule with no slug at all;` to §6 was green. Now: {adr_six_list_is_not_1_to_n_with_slugs: [['1','count'], … ['9','']]}. R12, the one that matters most, because a check that stops checking is worse than no check: the region this file is scanned through had no guard at all, so a comment quoting the end marker shrank it from 458 lines to ~20, stayed green, and masked a mis-pointed block label. The region is now verified before it is read — each marker exactly once in the file, and the three band functions defined inside it — and three ways of losing it went red: a marker-quoting comment {marker_counts: [1, 2], …}, the closing marker deleted {marker_counts: [1, 0], …}, and a band function moved below the marker {marker_counts: [1, 1], outside_the_region: ['_check_published_band_slack'], …}. That last one was green on the first attempt at the guard, because the names it looks for appear as string literals a few lines below and satisfied it from inside the region — the same self-reference the markers had; it matches `^def NAME(` now. PR #36 R16 found that guard pinning three names it had been told about and nothing about the region's edges — the exact case the comment beside it advertised. Both falsifications reproduced green first: a `_band_helper_probe` written after the end marker with `item 4 (derivation)` — a wrong slug — in its docstring, and the end marker moved to just below `def _check_published_band_slack() -> dict:`, which leaves all three named defs inside, keeps the counts at [1, 1], drops 111 lines and five references, and masks a mis-pointed reference in what it dropped. The guard reads EVERY band definition in the file and requires the closing marker to sit at a top-level boundary: {marker_counts: [1, 1], outside_the_region: ['_band_helper_probe'], markers_off_a_top_level_boundary: false, region_lines: 510} and {marker_counts: [1, 1], outside_the_region: [], markers_off_a_top_level_boundary: true, region_lines: 399}. The three round-2 mutations were re-watched against it and stay red, now naming all five band definitions rather than three. R17: the plural-range clause, dropped from this record by the round-2 rewrite while the behaviour stayed red — `§6 items 2-3 are what the check requires` gives {adr: reference_does_not_name_its_item, wrote: 'items 2', item_2_is: 'cited-run'}, and a range cannot carry one item's slug, which is why the form is refused rather than parsed. PR #36 R19/R20 — the membership test was a SUBSTRING test, and the comment warning against exactly that spelled `def _band_wrong(` inside the region, so that definition counted as inside wherever its body was. Falsification: `_band_wrong`'s 84-line body moved below the end marker returned {passed: True, wrong: []}. Membership is a byte offset now — nothing written in a comment can be one — and each of the five definitions moved below the marker in turn is red with its own name: {outside_the_region: ['_band_rule'], region_lines: 505}, ['_band_step_s'] 481, ['_band_wrong'] 426, ['_check_published_band'] 324, ['_check_published_band_slack'] 398. R20: only the closing edge was constrained, so moving the OPENING marker down to just above `_BAND_RATE` dropped the whole module-level block — three §6 references with it — while the counts stayed [1, 1] and every `def` stayed inside; green, and it masked a reference re-pointed inside the dropped block. The band set now includes the module-level constants and both markers must start their own line: that mutation gives {outside_the_region: ['_BAND_LINE', '_SLACK_MARK', '_SIX_ITEM', '_SIX_REF', '_REGION', '_BAND_DEF'], region_lines: 429}. The residue — module-level names outside the pinned set — is named in ADR-019 §6 and carried as T-R63. The remaining edge cases were watched in the same pass, so 'either marker' means both: the opening marker deleted {marker_counts: [0, 1], 13 strays}, quoted a second time {marker_counts: [2, 1], 13 strays}, and sharing a line with code {marker_counts: [1, 1], markers_off_a_top_level_boundary: true, region_lines: 510} — the last through the same top-level-line test, which is why its key covers both markers. That key was `end_marker_inside_a_body` while it only covered the closing marker; the outputs above are quoted under the name it carries now that it covers both.
